title: The Bhatts
hookLine: court poets whose swayyas praise the Gurus as one light (Swayye, ang 1389–1409)

lines: BARDS WHO PRAISED FOR A LIVING.
THEIR VERSES NEAR THE END OF THE GRANTH.
cards: A wedding toast. Somebody stands, clinks a glass, and praises the couple. Good toasts are a craft: specific, warm, a little grand.

Now take people whose whole trade was that craft, praising the great for a living, and send them into the court of the Gurus. That's who the Bhatts were, as tradition tells it: bards, poets of praise.
Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ang 1389, their verses fill page after page.

teach.h: SWAYYE: VERSES OF PRAISE, GURU BY GURU.
teach.b: Their verses are called swayye, after the swayya, a form of poem, and they're grouped by Guru: for the first Guru, the second, and on through the fifth. So the Bhatts aren't Bhagats from distant centuries.
Tradition places them in the time of Guru Arjan, looking at the line of Gurus and singing what they saw. And what they saw was one light.

One poet, Bhatt Mathura, lays it out in a single verse, in paraphrase: the Lord, in the form of light, was called Guru Nanak; from him came Angad, essence merged with essence; Angad set Amar Das firm; Amar Das gave Ram Das the royal canopy; now see Guru Arjan, the fifth.
Like a lamp lit from a lamp. Different bodies, the same light. Praise poetry can stop at the person: this king's sword, that king's wealth.
The Bhatts do praise the Gurus warmly, their wisdom, their steadiness, their nearness to God.

teach.h: NOT THE PERSON: WHAT PASSES BETWEEN.
teach.b: But underneath is a claim about what passes between them. Sikh readers hear these verses as a witness, from outside the family, to the teaching that the Guru is one, whatever body the light is in.

They also close a week of the Granth's other voices: Sadhna pleading for grace, Ramanand at home in a house colored with love, Parmanand asking what the hearing was for, Surdas and his one line, Jaidev the old poet, Bhikhan's medicine.
And now the Bhatts, who brought their trade of praise to the Gurus and used it to point at the light.

how: The Bhatts' swayye are read and sung in the Guru Granth Sahib like the rest of Gurbani, and Sikhs turn to them for the teaching that the light of Guru Nanak passed whole from Guru to Guru.

games.q: you're a bard whose trade is praising the great. you arrive at the Guru's court. what does your praise land on?
o: the one light passed from Guru to Guru.
games.why: the Bhatts praise the Gurus warmly, but underneath is one claim: the same light, lamp from lamp, in each.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose goodness you've seen up close: not their looks or success, but patience, honesty, a kindness nobody noticed.
Like a Bhatt, be specific: find the exact moment you saw it, then look for what's underneath, the light in them that isn't only theirs. If you pray, breathe out Waheguru.
